item.title: UNHCR Ukraine Factsheet, September 2026
item.description:
Country: Ukraine
Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

Please refer to the attached file.

Life-saving assistance & protection: UNHCR delivers critical humanitarian assistance and protection to evacuated and other newly displaced people, as well as to war-affected people in frontline areas facing hostilities, and those impacted by aerial attacks.

Supporting IDPs with vulnerabilities in protracted displacement: UNHCR provides protection services and humanitarian assistance to IDPs through targeted programmes to promote access to rights, dignified accommodation, and durable solutions.

Durable solutions and recovery: UNHCR contributes to recovery and durable solutions through community based, psychosocial, and legal protection programmes, repair of homes and support to access inclusive social protection services.

HIGHLIGHTS

Emergency shelter: Since the beginning of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, UNHCR has supported over 665,000 people across the country with emergency shelter kits and materials immediately after attacks. For more info, see the 2026 Q2 Shelter & Housing Factsheet here.

Cash assistance is one of the most efficient and effective ways to support people adversely impacted by the war in Ukraine. Between January - August 2026, UNHCR disbursed multipurpose cash assistance to almost 128,478 people with specific needs. Since March 2022, UNHCR has provided cash assistance to more than 2.5 million people in Ukraine, totaling $748 million. For more info, see the 2026 Q2 Cash Assistance Factsheet here.

Winter response: To prevent further displacement and help people remain safe and warm in their homes, UNHCR launched a comprehensive winter response plan for 2026-27 as a part of a broader UN inter-agency appeal.
item.author: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

item.title: UNHCR Latvia Factsheet, September 2026
item.description:
Countries: Latvia, Ukraine
Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

Please refer to the attached file.

During 2026, the number of refugees from Ukraine under Temporary Protection, at almost 32,000, remained broadly unchanged, reflecting continued new arrivals alongside onward movements to other countries.

UNHCR continues to collaborate with state authorities to improve access to asylum for those irregularly arriving in the southeastern regions bordering Belarus

UNHCR supports the government of Latvia to strengthen protection measures for forcibly displaced people while aligning with the goals of the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum

HIGHLIGHTS

Implementation of the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum

UNHCR supports the Latvian government in its implementation of the EU Pact through advocacy and capacity building and by providing recommendations on draft legislation in the areas of vulnerability screening, detention, legal aid and counselling, as well as the national monitoring mechanism.

Access to asylum at the Latvia-Belarus border According to the State Border

Guard, the number of bordercrossing attempts that were prevented, remained high during the first eight months of 2026, with over 10,400 denied entries compared to over 12,400 during the same period in 2025. UNHCR conducted regular monitoring of the border, as well as detention and reception centers, and where necessary, brought observations to the attention of the management of the centers and the State Border Guard.

item.title: UNHCR Sweden Fact Sheet, September 2026
item.description:
Countries: Sweden, Afghanistan, Iraq, Syrian Arab Republic, Ukraine
Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

Please refer to the attached file.

Asylum system: Sweden has made strong contributions to refugee protection through a well-established asylum system and policy support. The asylum system has been reformed in light of the implementation of the EU Pact as of the summer of 2026.

Contributor of unearmarked funding: Sweden is UNHCR’s largest contributor of unearmarked funding. Sweden’s total contribution to UNHCR in 2025 amounted to USD 159.4 million.

Stable and secure status: UNHCR advocates for Sweden to grant all beneficiaries of international protection a secure and stable status to facilitate integration.

HIGHLIGHTS

Fewer asylum applications and returns

The Swedish Migration Agency reported that by August 2026, asylum applications in Sweden had fallen by over 40% compared to the previous year, while returns also decreased. These figures indicate a continued shift in the protection environment in Sweden, against the backdrop of significant policy and legislative changes affecting the asylum and reception system.

UNHCR voluntary repatriation counselling

Since August 2026, UNHCR has provided counselling services for refugees considering voluntary repatriation, funded by the Swedish Migration Agency. Through provision of independent counselling and reliable information on the repatriation process and conditions in countries of origin, UNHCR helps refugees understand their options and make informed decisions

item.title: UNHCR Austria Factsheet, September 2026
item.description:
Countries: Austria, Afghanistan, Syrian Arab Republic, Türkiye, Ukraine, World
Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

Please refer to the attached file.

Statistics for 2025 show a further decrease in asylum applications, with a total of around 16,700 asylum applications compared to 25,360 cases in 2024.

In 2025, only 42 per cent were new applications, others included children born to refugees and repeat applications. The downward trend continued in 2026 with 6,500 applications by 31 August.

Austria is among the top donors to UNHCR’s activities, while supporting the international responses to the needs of forcibly displaced people worldwide.

HIGHLIGHTS

2 new AMIF projects granted

The office successfully applied for 2 AMIF projects. Both the continuation of the quality assurance project “Bridge” as well as the new voluntary return project for protection holders from Syria (PARRS) were granted.

75th anniversary of the Refugee Convention

The Office highlighted the Convention’s enduring importance through a variety of projects. The Convention was discussed in the media, including in a radio series featuring the Head of Office. Stakeholders and multipliers, including teachers, students and NGOs, received briefings and materials on the Convention and refugee protection. The Office also participated in several events, including panel discussions, lectures and high-level meetings (see below), focusing on the Convention.
item.author: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

item.title: UNHCR Albania Fact Sheet, September 2026
item.description:
Countries: Albania, Serbia, Syrian Arab Republic, Ukraine
Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

Please refer to the attached file.

UNHCR advocates for a strengthened national asylum system and contributes to further developing the capacity of government authorities to align asylum laws and practices with international and EU law.

UNHCR works with municipalities to strengthen the socio-economic inclusion of refugees and asylum-seekers by improving access to livelihoods, social protection and local services.

UNHCR’s work in Albania is supported by the EU-funded EU4Migration project and the PSMM3 Regional Programme.

HIGHLIGHTS

Socio-economic inclusion

UNHCR continues to work with the municipalities of Korça and Gjirokastra to strengthen the socio-economic inclusion of refugees and asylum-seekers. This collaboration aims to address barriers to decent livelihoods and access to social protection rights and schemes. UNHCR also advocates for their inclusion in the local social care systems of both municipalities.

Strengthening asylum decision-making

In July 2026, UNHCR organized a workshop on drafting asylum decisions to strengthen authorities’ practical skills in fact-finding, credibility assessment and legal analysis. The workshop helped participants develop the skills needed to draft legally sound, well-reasoned and evidence-based decisions. It also promoted exchanges of experience and a shared understanding of asylum decision-making standards among participating institutions.

item.title: UNHCR Romania Fact Sheet, September 2026
item.description:
Countries: Romania, Afghanistan, Syrian Arab Republic, Ukraine
Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

Please refer to the attached file.

UNHCR supports the government’s response to protect and include refugees in Romania through initiatives fostering inclusion and self-reliance, protection services, counselling and targeted assistance.

Romania granted access to social benefits for refugees from Ukraine, through the Emergency Ordinance No. 96 on 28 June 2024, thereby addressing the needs of vulnerable refugees, to the same extent as Romanian citizens.

UNHCR leads Inter-Agency coordination, supporting the national response, with 43 Refugee Response Plan partners ensuring alignment and synergy with the Government’s policy and localization.

HIGHLIGHTS

Life-saving assistance

So far in 2026, UNHCR distributed 4,998 core relief items (CRIs), including blankets, bedding, clothing, and hygiene kits to 631 people in need.

Protection information and counselling

In 2026, UNHCR and partners have provided over 6,148 refugees with information and counselling in person or by phone. In addition, some 21,200 refugees are regularly reached through social media dedicated channels, including UNHCR’s Telegram channel, amplifying UNHCR’s messages to nearly 80,000 refugees.

Delivering together

UNHCR hosts 12 partners and national authorities at the RomExpo Community Centre in Bucharest, visited by over 100 refugees daily. The centre serves as a main “one-stop shop” for refugees. UNHCR is also hosting the social shop run by the Municipality of Bucharest.

item.title: UNHCR Belarus Factsheet, September 2026
item.description:
Countries: Belarus, Afghanistan, Georgia, Ukraine
Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

Please refer to the attached file.

Access to asylum: UNHCR works towards enhancing the asylum space and standardization of the state Refugee Status Determination Procedure (SRSDP) through capacity building and liaison with asylum authorities at country and regional levels.

Self-reliance and inclusion: UNHCR promotes inclusive and sustainable integration aligned with the UN Country Framework 2026–2030, aiming to expand the access of forcibly displaced and stateless people to national social protection systems.

Since 1 January 2026, UNHCR’s operations in Belarus and the Russian Federation have been consolidated under a Multi‑Country Office (MCO).

HIGHLIGHTS

UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework

On 23 June, the MFA of Belarus and the UN Country Team gathered to present to both the diplomatic community and the business sector in Belarus, strategic directions of their commitments and priorities in accordance with the five-year UNSDCF. UNHCR presented its priorities, focusing on longterm solutions for integration, emphasizing the role of the private sector to support inclusion of refugees in economic activities and promote self-reliance.

Protection Monitoring Missions

In 2026, UNHCR conducted three field missions across Belarus to monitor the protection situation, engage with regional authorities and learn first-hand information from refugees and asylum-seekers. These missions included visits to state-run accommodation centres for asylum-seekers in Vitebsk and Gomel, as well as a joint mission with the State Border Committee to the Brest region at the Belarus–Poland border.

item.title: UNHCR Spain Fact Sheet, September 2026
item.description:
Countries: Spain, Colombia, Ukraine, Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of), World
Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

Please refer to the attached file.

From 1 January to 31 August, 20,417 people arrived in Spain by sea and land, 13% fewer than during the same period in 2025. Around 75% arrived through the Western Mediterranean route, while 25% arrived through the West Africa Atlantic route.

During the first five months of 2026, around 50,300 people applied for asylum in Spain, 22% fewer than during the same period in 2025. The main nationalities were Venezuelan (58%), Malian (15%) and Colombian (7%).

As of 31 May 2026, Spain had received 274,597 applications for temporary protection since March 2022, including 2,222 applications during January–May 2026. Of the applications submitted in 2026, 41% were from men, 41% from women, 10% from boys and 8% from girls.

HIGHLIGHTS

Queen Letizia of Spain receives UNHCR delegation and refugees

Queen Letizia of Spain received a UNHCR delegation at the Zarzuela Palace, accompanied by refugees supported by UNHCR. The audience focused on the situation of refugees and asylum-seekers in Spain and UNHCR’s work to promote their rights and access to international protection. Read more here.

Other stories: UNHCR served on the jury of a storytelling competition for refugee and migrant women organized by Nebrija Global Chair on Spanish as a language of migrants and refugees, helping promote women’s refugee voices through literature. The initiative culminated in a publication of selected stories featuring a foreword by UNHCR.

item.title: UNHCR Switzerland Fact Sheet, September 2026
item.description:
Countries: Switzerland, Afghanistan, Eritrea, Ukraine, World
Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

Please refer to the attached file.

As of mid-2026, there are 211,381 refugees (96,201 with refugee status, 41,913 with complementary protection and 73,267 with temporary protection status S), 15,506 asylum seekers as well as 1,407 stateless persons in Switzerland. Switzerland estimates around 22,000 asylum applications for 2026 overall, down from 25,000 in 2025.

UNHCR is engaged in the development of a new Asylum Strategy 2027 and works with authorities and NGOs to further strengthen the quality of the asylum system and the socio-economic inclusion of refugees.

Switzerland remains a strong supporter of UNHCR, both as host of UNHCR’s headquarters and a top donor, providing flexible and predictable multi-year funding.

HIGHLIGHTS

A NEW CHAPTER FOR UNHCR SWITZERLAND AND LIECHTENSTEIN

Since 1 July, the UNHCR Office for Switzerland and Liechtenstein has been operating with a significantly streamlined structure and now comprises only two staff. Despite limited resources, the Office continues to fulfil its core functions in dialogue, policy engagement and advocacy, monitoring developments in the asylum and refugee context, and fostering cooperation with government counterparts, civil society, academia, refugees, and other key stakeholders.

PATH2WORK

Path2Work became a UNHCR-Partner. Through the partnership between Path2Work and UNHCR, bridges are being built between refugee talent and employers, creating new career opportunities and laying the foundations for sustainable integration. Currently, 15,000 users are registered on the digital platform, with a further 17,000 people set to be invited to join from October. Access to the labour market fosters self-reliance, inclusion, and meaningful participation in society.

item.title: UNHCR Cyprus Factsheet, September 2026
item.description:
Countries: Cyprus, Cameroon, Democratic Republic of the Congo, occupied Palestinian territory, Syrian Arab Republic, Ukraine
Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

Please refer to the attached file.

UNHCR provides legal and technical advice, monitors the asylum system and supports protection-sensitive implementation of the EU Pact. In the northern part of Cyprus, where no formal asylum system exists, UNHCR conducts RSD under its mandate and works with partners to help refugees and asylumseekers access their rights.

Across the island, UNHCR maintains direct communication with refugee communities and supports access to legal counselling, psychosocial assistance, promoting inclusion and selfreliance.

UNHCR works across Cyprus to ensure access to international protection, prevent refoulement and promote the rights of forcibly displaced and stateless people.

HIGHLIGHTS

Implementing major asylum reforms

Cyprus is moving from policy design to implementation of the EU Pact. UNHCR provides legal advice during the adoption of the legislation and targeted training to asylum service officers, social workers, the judiciary, police and other key stakeholders to support fair, efficient and protection-sensitive asylum processes.

Preserving legal and social counselling

UNHCR is working with the Government to maintain essential counselling during institutional transition, helping avoid service gaps and ensure continued access to information, referrals and support.

Supporting self-reliance

At Kofinou Reception Centre, UNHCR supports the transition from reception to independent living through counselling, employment support and housing assistance, strengthening inclusion and easing pressure on the reception system.

Building public support for refugee protection

Through World Refugee Day initiatives and activities for the 75th anniversary of the Refugee Convention, UNHCR supported community activities across Cyprus that promoted refugee participation, social cohesion and understanding of refugee protection.

item.title: UNHCR Italy Factsheet, September 2026
item.description:
Countries: Italy, Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Peru, Syrian Arab Republic, Ukraine, World
Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

Please refer to the attached file.

Italy has been party to the 1951 Refugee Convention since 1954, when UNHCR established its first presence. In 2026, UNHCR’s presence in Italy forms part of the Rome-based Multi-Country Office, which also covers the Holy See, Malta and San Marino and provides operational support to Cyprus.

UNHCR supports Italy in strengthening a fair and efficient asylum system, including through technical assistance in the implementation of the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum, in line with international standards.

Partnering with government, civil society, the academia and private sector, UNHCR works to expand safe and legal pathways that provide protection and durable solutions: resettlement, humanitarian corridors, humanitarian evacuations, and pathways for education and employment.

HIGHLIGHTS

ARRIVALS BY LAND AND SEA

In 2026, as of end-June, 14,388 people had arrived in Italy by sea - the largest number in Southern Europe - and a decrease of 52 per cent compared to the same period in 2025. Nearly 83 per cent had departed from Libya, whilst the rest from Algeria, Tunisia and Türkiye. Around 3,000 people were intercepted at the north-eastern land border with Slovenia — a slight increase compared to 2025—although UNHCR estimates that many more crossings went undetected.

STABILIZATION AND SOLUTIONS INITIATIVE

Through the Stabilization and Solutions Initiative, Italy and UNHCR are developing a structured cooperation platform to support refugee-hosting countries along key displacement routes. Anchored in UNHCR’s 50 by 35 vision, the Initiative connects Italy’s engagement in Africa with efforts to reduce long-term aid dependency in refugee-hosting areas. A first phase will focus on Chad, Mauritania, Niger and Sudan, supporting area-based interventions to strengthen local services, livelihoods, national systems and social cohesion. By linking development cooperation, route-based protection, asylum-system strengthening and safe pathways, the Initiative reflects Italy’s whole-of-government approach and offers a scalable model to align migration, development and stabilization objectives with solutions for refugees and host countries.

item.title: UNHCR Greece Factsheet - September 2026
item.description:
Countries: Greece, Afghanistan, Egypt, Syrian Arab Republic, Ukraine
Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

Please refer to the attached file.

As one of the EU’s main external border countries, Greece remains at the forefront of mixed movements of refugees and migrants, managing sustained migratory pressures. In this context, UNHCR’s presence and protection role are vital.

UNHCR works with authorities, civil society, partners and refugee communities to promote a favourable protection environment and advance sustainable responses for refugees, asylum-seekers and stateless people.

UNHCR provides information, counselling, legal assistance, referrals, integration programmes, and technical expertise on asylum, reception and inclusion, including on the EU Pact’s implementation.

HIGHLIGHTS

Refugee Women Academy (RWA)

In September 2026, UNHCR and Piraeus Bank launched the new RWA cycle, providing vocational training for refugee and asylum-seeking women in high-demand sectors in Greece such as hospitality, tourism and food services. Currently implemented by METAdrasi and the Greek chapter of the International Women’s Coffee Alliance, the Academy has trained 273 women since 2023, with nearly one in three graduates securing employment within six months.

UNHCR-UNESCO Taekwondo Open Summer School

In August 2026, 44 children and adolescents, including unaccompanied children and host community members, participated in a Taekwondo Open Summer School in Lesvos led by a coach from the Republic of Korea to promote respect, well-being and inclusion through sport. The initiative, jointly led by UNHCR and the UNESCO International Centre of Martial Arts, was delivered with NGOs Yoga and Sport with Refugees and Iliaktida, with support from the Ministry of Migration and Asylum and the Embassy of the Republic of Korea in Greece.

item.title: UNHCR Iceland Fact Sheet, September 2026
item.description:
Countries: Iceland, occupied Palestinian territory, Ukraine, Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of), World
Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

Please refer to the attached file.

Contributions to international protection: Iceland maintains a favourable protection environment for forcibly displaced and stateless people and continues to explore modalities to strengthen protection.

Increase of funding: Iceland has responded to rising displacement needs globally by increasing its funding to UNHCR. So far, in 2026, Iceland contributed USD 5.2 million to UNHCR.

Access to procedures: Iceland ensures effective access to asylum procedures for forcibly displaced people, including beneficiaries of temporary protection.

HIGHLIGHTS

Harmonization with neighbouring countries

In line with the “Platform for the Coalition Government”, authorities are reviewing migration and asylum law in Iceland to harmonize it with neighboring countries.

Implementation of the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum

Although Iceland is not an EU Member State, it participates in parts of the European asylum architecture. Iceland has been preparing legislative amendments to incorporate relevant Pact provisions, including, screening, asylum and migration management rules and Eurodac reforms.

Collective protection

The collective protection scheme for persons fleeing Ukraine following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has been extended until March 2027 with a proposal for further extension until March 2028 pending in Parliament.

item.title: World: New day to end child marriage must result in action
item.description:
Countries: World, Bangladesh, Uganda
Source: Plan International

12 million girls still marry before the age of 18 every year

27 November 2026

While the first UN International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage and Unions brings much needed recognition of this harmful practice, awareness is not enough. Governments worldwide need to enforce existing laws, invest in girls' education and tackle the root causes of child marriage so all girls can decide their futures.

Plan International has welcomed the establishment of the first UN International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage and Unions (CEFMU), to be marked on 27 November, but warns that international recognition must translate into urgent action.

With 12 million girls still married before the age of 18 every year, Plan is calling on governments worldwide to strengthen protections, enforce existing laws and invest in solutions that enable girls to decide their own futures.

“We are very proud to see the first International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage become a reality. This historic milestone reflects years of tireless advocacy by girls, activists and organisations around the world, including by Plan International.

“This marks an important step forward for girls’ rights, bringing much-needed global attention to harmful practices that continues to affect millions of girls. But awareness alone is not enough. Every 3 seconds, a girl is married before she turns 18.

“The world is running out of time to end child marriage by 2030. It is time to deliver on that promise.

“Governments must use this moment to turn recognition into action. That means enforcing laws that protect girls, investing in their education and tackling the root causes of child marriage. Above all, it means making sure girls themselves have a say in the decisions that shape their lives,” said Reena Ghelani, Plan International’s Chief Executive Officer.

Child marriage persistently violates girls’ rights

Whilst the proportion of girls married before the age of 18 has fallen globally from nearly 1 in 4 to 1 in 5 over the past 25 years, progress has been uneven, and it remains one of the most persistent violations of girls’ rights.

According to Girl Goals: What has changed for girls?, a report co-authored by Plan International, UNICEF and UN Women in 2025, South Asia has made considerable progress in reducing child marriage. Progress in Latin America and the Caribbean has been modest as data released this year says prevalence in the region declined by just 2.6% between 2005 and 2025. However, no country has yet met the Sustainable Development Goal target of eliminating child marriage.

For the millions of girls who are still married as children, the consequences can last a lifetime. Child, early and forced marriages are linked to violence, early pregnancy and associated health risks, and can disrupt girls’ education and limit their economic opportunities.

“My stepmother wanted me to get married, because she felt it was a burden for them to look after me. She arranged my marriage and I became a mother at a very young age. As my body was still developing, I had a complicated pregnancy. I was bedridden for 4 months, until I gave birth. It is a miracle that my daughter came into this world”, recalled Noor*, a 15-year-old girl living in the southwest of Bangladesh who was married at 12 to a 22-year-old man.

Action required at every level to end child marriage

Plan International’s State of the World’s Girls research found that 1 in 4 girls and young women surveyed had no say in the decision to marry. This highlights why legal protections, while essential to prevent coercion, violence and exploitation, must be accompanied by action to address the inequalities and social norms that deny girls control over their own lives. Neither legislation nor international commitments alone can end CEFMU.

Plan International has worked for decades alongside girls, young people, communities and governments to prevent child marriage, support girls affected by it and challenge the inequalities that allow it to persist. Ending child marriage requires action at every level: empowering girls to exercise their rights, working with families and communities to challenge harmful social norms, and strengthening the laws, policies and services that protect girls.

Although child marriage remains deeply rooted in many communities around the world, with 46% of girls who took part in the study citing economic hardship or social and family pressure as the most common reasons for entering into a marriage or union, Plan International’s experience shows that working within and alongside communities can have a positive effect. In Uganda, for example, support among parents, caregivers and families for young people making their own decisions about marriage increased from 56% to 90% during a Plan International-supported project.

“Child marriage is not inevitable. It is preventable. Girls need real choices, real opportunities and the freedom to decide their own futures. The success of this new international day will not be measured by speeches or statements, but by whether fewer girls are forced into marriage and more are able to stay in school, exercise their rights and choose their own futures,” Reena Ghelani said.

*Names changed to protect identities.

What happens after a girl marries as a child?

251 girls and young women from 15 countries shared their personal stories of child marriage and its lasting impact with us.

Through their stories, the price of child marriage becomes clear:

  • Violence
  • Domestic drudgery
  • Difficulty staying in school
  • Loss of control over all aspects of life – including if or when to have children.

What about the policy and legal reforms restricting child marriage? Once married or in a relationship, numerous girls told us they have meant very little – many are still trapped.

More needs to happen to protect girls from, and after, child marriage. And girls know what they need.

item.title: UNHCR Afghanistan Situation Regional Update October 2026
item.description:
Countries: Afghanistan, Iran (Islamic Republic of), Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Tajikistan
Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

Please refer to the attached file.

OPERATIONAL CONTEXT

The operational environment in Afghanistan was shaped by localized security dynamics, access constraints and operational capacity challenges. In the south, the security situation remained generally calm, although reported security incidents increased during the second half of the month. At Torkham, access constraints affecting humanitarian actors' engagement with deportees limited protection screening. Humanitarian activities resumed after border clashes in late October, although access to Torkham Zero Point remained suspended at month-end.

Regional tensions and economic pressures continued in Iran amid an uncertain security environment and ongoing diplomatic efforts to prevent renewed escalation. Many refugees and other forcibly displaced people faced economic hardship, insecure livelihoods and barriers to essential services, which were compounded by the socioeconomic impacts of the regional conflict. Disruptions to crossborder trade with Pakistan further affected the movement of commercial goods and essential commodities. Despite localized security and weather-related incidents, including flooding in north and north-east Iran, UNHCR operations continued across the country.

Unrest and security incidents continued to disrupt UN movements and humanitarian access across Pakistan. In Islamabad, Rawalpindi and Punjab, heightened security measures and road closures caused intermittent movement disruptions. In Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, security incidents increased by around 10% compared with September, with continued attacks against security forces raising concerns about the safety of humanitarian personnel and infrastructure. Political developments also temporarily disrupted UN operations. In Balochistan, militant activity and movement restrictions in parts of Kalat and Rakhshan limited humanitarian access and field monitoring. In Sindh, enforcement measures against undocumented Afghan nationals continued, although the overall situation remained relatively stable.

Across Central Asia, protection environments remained mixed, with some progress in strengthening national rights frameworks alongside persistent barriers to refugee protection, particularly in access to territory and essential services. In Tajikistan, ratification of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities marked progress towards advancing the rights of people with disabilities, with a national action plan to follow. However, reported forced returns of Afghan nationals, including refugees and asylumseekers, without due process, legal assistance or opportunities to appeal remained a significant protection concern.

item.title: World: Factsheet 2026: Education Aid Cuts Are Jeopardizing the Future of Children with Disabilities - A call to action for donors
item.description:
Country: World
Source: Humanity & Inclusion

Please refer to the attached file.

KEY NUMBERS

−22.2% Projected fall in net bilateral ODA for education, 2024– 2026

−15.3% Decrease in direct ODA to basic education, 2023–2024

Over 17 million Children with disabilities counted amongst out-ofschool children in crisis contexts

70.6% of DAC members’ bilateral education commitments with no recorded disability objective in 2024

−38.4% Fall in DAC members’ bilateral education commitments recorded with disability inclusion as the principal objective between 2023–2024

– reaching 0,5% in 2024 49% more likely for children with disabilities to have never attended school, than children without disabilities

Education is increasingly sidelined in donor priorities

The latest wave of aid cuts is accelerating a longer-term erosion of education’s place in donor priorities. Between 2010 and 2024, education’s share of total aid fell from 14% to 9% for the World Bank, from 14% to 11% for France, from 10% to 3% for Germany, and from 8% to 3% for Japan. The European Union is a notable exception, with education’s share increasing from around 5-6% in the mid-2010s to approximately 10% in recent years.

The OECD projects that net bilateral education aid from DAC members will decline by 22.2% between 2024 and 2026.3 Between 2023 and 2024 alone, the education's share of sectorallocable ODA fell from 8.4% to 7.5%, marking the lowest level recorded since 2010. Some of the largest reductions came from major providers, including Germany (−USD 514 million, −45.6%), World Bank International Development Association (IDA) (−USD 368 million, −14.0%), and UNRWA (−USD 206 million, −29.8%).

Education is increasingly competing with immediate humanitarian needs, geopolitical priorities and areas perceived to offer more direct strategic or commercial returns to donors. The growing emphasis on “mutual benefits” and national interest in development cooperation may further disadvantage education. Investments in public education systems generate primarily long-term benefits for people and economies in partner countries, rather than immediate or readily identifiable returns for donor countries.

This decline is particularly alarming given the extreme concentration of education aid among a handful of donors. Nearly half of all global education aid is provided by just five actors: Germany, the World Bank's IDA, France, the United States and EU institutions.5 As a result, decisions taken by a small number of major donors can trigger system-wide shocks across education systems, especially in countries that remain highly dependent on external financing. ODA finances an average of 17% of public education expenditure in low-income countries, rising to 31% in Sierra Leone and as much as 40% in Rwanda.6 In contexts where domestic resources are already insufficient to meet growing education needs, aid cuts threaten teacher recruitment and training, learning materials, school accessibility measures, and targeted support services that enable children with disabilities to attend and succeed in school.
item.author: Humanity & Inclusion

item.title: World: Factsheet 2026: Health Aid Cuts Are Putting Global Health Equity at Risk - A call to action for donors
item.description:
Country: World
Source: Humanity & Inclusion

Please refer to the attached file.

KEY NUMBERS

−29% to −46% Projected fall in net bilateral ODA for health and population, 2024-2026, representing a reduction of USD 5-8 bn

−13.8% Fall in official-donor health ODA grant-equivalent flows, 2023–2024

1.1% of total bilateral health ODA was recorded with disability inclusion as the principal objective in 2024

50% more likely for persons with disabilities to face catastrophic health expenditures

86% of OPDs report assistivetechnology and rehabilitation services becoming less accessible due to aid cuts

3 times more likely for persons with disabilities to be denied the needed healthcare

A general collapse with some exception on the cover page

Global health aid is contracting sharply. Net bilateral ODA for health and population is projected to fall by 29-46% between 2024 and 2026, equivalent to roughly USD 5-8 billion, following a 13.8% decline between 2023 and 2024.2 Under the higher-cut scenario, health ODA in 2026 would fall to levels last seen around 2008: that is up to one-third below 2019 levels and 63% below the 2022 peak.

Health aid is highly concentrated. In 2024, the five largest individual donors (the United States, the United Kingdom, Japan, Germany, and France) accounted for approximately 60.9% of officialdonor health ODA grant-equivalent flows to developing countries. Decisions by a small number of donors can therefore materially alter the global health-financing landscape. While non-DAC donors increased their health financing by 33.3% in 2024, these gains were insufficient to offset the much larger reductions among traditional bilateral donors.

The contraction is affecting specific health functions. In 2024, global ODA declined by 25.4% for health-personnel development, 25% for basic nutrition, 24.1% for basic health, 18.9% for infectious-disease control and 6.6% for medical services.

item.title: Venezuela – Terremoto: Lineamientos Técnicos Kits de Enseres Esenciales para el Hogar (EHI) (noviembre 2026 - Version 1.0)
item.description:
Country: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of)
Sources: CCCM Cluster, International Organization for Migration, Shelter Cluster, UN High Commissioner for Refugees

Please refer to the attached file.

1.Contexto

Los terremotos consecutivos de magnitud 7,2 y 7,5 que sacudieron el centro-norte de Venezuela el 24 de junio de 2026 ocasionaron una destrucción generalizada de viviendas, infraestructura pública y servicios esenciales en siete estados: La Guaira, Distrito Capital, Miranda, Aragua, Carabobo, Falcón y Yaracuy.

Además de los daños estructurales, la emergencia ha provocado una pérdida generalizada de enseres esenciales para el hogar (EHI), reduciendo la capacidad de las familias para mantener un espacio doméstico funcional. La falta de artículos básicos compromete funciones esenciales de la vida cotidiana, tales como, dormir, cocinar, almacenar agua y comida, acceder a iluminación o electricidad, y realizar prácticas de higiene personal. La ausencia de estos artículos no solo limita la habitabilidad, sino que también afecta la salubridad, protección y la dignidad de las familias.

En este escenario, la provisión de kits de enseres esenciales (EHIs) se convierte en un componente clave de la respuesta humanitaria, al garantizar que las personas puedan vivir adecuadamente y con dignidad en sus viviendas, facilitando la recuperación temprana y el retorno seguro a los hogares en las comunidades afectadas.
